> "Half the time when I try to connect to baby me, I feel fake and it seems crazy."
after: (Not written yet. Next comes a new heading, "The Parent You Inherited". Its first paragraph: before you ever set out to build the Nurturer, Protector and Guide, you already have a way of treating yourself that you learned from how you were treated. Don't say any of that here.)
brief:
- right after Scott's quote, and the last paragraph before the new heading "The Parent You Inherited"
- what it says: keeping at it does help. If your little one learned to expect being dropped, one sitting isn't going to win their trust. But keeping at it doesn't explain why the whole thing can feel fake.
- The article already has, in Make a Simple Vow: "one beautiful session wouldn't convince me either". Keep the one-sitting point to a few words or leave it out.
- Don't say what Joel used to think or believe: his own words don't say it. Don't add anything about Scott beyond his quote.
- End on why it feels fake as an open question, without announcing what comes next.
length: two or three sentences, 35 to 70 words
voice: in the second person like the article, with Joel's first person only for what he thinks now ("I think")
guide_passage: I used to think the answer was mainly persistence: keep showing up and eventually the child will trust you. There’s some truth in that. A child expecting abandonment probably won’t place full confidence in one meditation. Persistence alone still misses what is happening when the whole thing feels fake.
next: Before you deliberately build the Nurturer, Protector, and Guide, you usually already have a learned way of treating yourself: the inner parent “script” you inherited from how you were treated. It may show up as words, feelings, expectations, or habits rather than a literal inner voice. It can be warm, but for many people its first version is a critic or warden: don’t cry, don’t be needy, don’t get angry, don’t embarrass us, don’t become too independent. Piece by piece, the child learns which qualities have to disappear from view to preserve belonging.
